name: Tartaric acid

lead: Tartaric acid is a natural acid found in grapes and wine by-products. It is one of the alpha-hydroxy acids (AHAs), alongside glycolic, lactic, malic and citric acid, used in cosmetic formulations.
In skincare it appears in exfoliating peels and blends, where it helps loosen dead surface cells for smoother, brighter skin.

paras: It is typically one component in AHA products such as peels and exfoliants, often with glycolic or lactic acid. It is used topically on a periodic basis.
AHAs can cause swelling, burning and itching, and research is mixed on whether they raise or lower sun damage depending on concentration.

angle.text: As an AHA, tartaric acid is included in peels and exfoliants to smooth the skin surface.

lead: Tartaric acid is a white crystalline organic acid and alpha-hydroxy acid found in grapes, tamarind, bananas and citrus; commercially it is mostly the L-(+) form, a by-product of winemaking.[1]

AHAs including tartaric acid are used extensively in cosmetic formulations and as superficial peeling agents, and in dermatology for keratoses and acne.[2] Tartaric acid is usually a supporting ingredient in blends.
A review found AHAs act dually on skin and that their effect on photodamage depends on concentration.[2]

paras: It exists as L-(+), D-(-) and meso forms.[1] Winemakers knew the crude crystals for centuries; Scheele developed chemical extraction in 1769, and Pasteur's 1847 work on its salts was important to the discovery of chirality.[1]
AHAs are used as superficial peeling agents and to improve the appearance of keratoses and acne.[2] Adverse reactions include swelling, burning and itching.[2]

It is a food antioxidant and sourness agent (E334), a baking-powder component and a chelating agent; it is well tolerated by humans though toxic at high doses, and is classified as causing serious eye damage.[1]
No studies found specific to tartaric acid alone. A review of AHAs in general covers keratinocyte and animal-model mechanisms.[2]

timeline.event: Scheele and colleagues develop extraction and purification.[1]
Pasteur's work on tartrate crystals leads to pure L-tartaric acid.[1]
